case_study_insert.main_stem: VitalCore Fitness (VCF) is a private limited company in the leisure and fitness sector, employing a workforce of 35. Founded in 2015 by Nadia Rahman, it runs two city gyms and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. VCF plans to invest $620,000 in two new gym sites with automated access technology and an e-commerce booking app, financed by a $380,000 ten-year bank loan, $160,000 retained profit and $80,000 from the sale of old equipment. It has fixed costs of $240,000 a year, a variable cost of $12 a unit and a selling price of $42 for a membership unit, and currently delivers 15,000 units a year. VCF faces two problems: absenteeism has reached 8%, and 6% of fitness equipment is out of service at any time.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations Log — Q3 2025: The two existing gyms logged 3,600 member visits last week with 14 equipment breakdowns, a 6% equipment downtime rate. Member complaints rose from 19 to 34 per month. Average waiting time for a gym induction is 5.4 days. A survey of 700 members found that 62% would pay $6 more for 24-hour access through the new e-commerce booking app, and 49% used the app weekly. 9 of 35 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the automated access technology; a manufacturer course costs $420 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of VitalCore Fitness for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.0% to 4.5%, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans such as VCF's $380,000 expansion loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.4% from $12.80 to $13.62 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills for gym and reception staff. (3) Imported gym equipment prices have risen 11.3% because of a weaker dollar, while consumer spending on leisure memberships grew 4.2% over the same period.

questions.question_text: VCF is funding its $620,000 expansion with a $380,000 bank loan, $160,000 retained profit and $80,000 from the sale of old equipment. Explain two advantages for VCF of using the $80,000 from the sale of old equipment rather than borrowing more.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Selling old equipment raises $80,000 without adding interest or repayment obligations, so VCF avoids increasing the $380,000 loan while meeting fixed costs of $240,000 a year. The cash can go straight into the automated access technology and e-commerce app, and every dollar saved in finance charges helps absorb the 11.3% increase in imported equipment prices.

Point 2: Releasing cash tied up in outdated machines improves liquidity at a time when 6% of equipment is out of service and 34 members a month are complaining. Unlike a larger loan, the sale has no collateral requirement, so the two new gym sites are not at risk of repossession if the 15,000 membership units are not achieved. It also reduces dependence on external finance for Nadia Rahman's business, leaving the $160,000 retained profit available for the disruption of opening new sites. Selling outdated kit also frees floor space in the two existing gyms for the new access technology, reducing disruption while the $620,000 programme is installed.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to VCF's expansion, equipment and costs.

questions.question_text: VCF's complaints rose from 19 to 34 a month. Consider local radio advertising, social media influencer marketing, or discounted trial memberships. Which should VCF choose to attract new members? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Local radio advertising: Radio can quickly reach commuters in both city catchments and promote the two new gym sites. However, airtime is costly, the message is generic and most listeners are outside the immediate catchment of the existing gyms, so much of the spend is wasted for a 35-employee operator already committing $620,000 to expansion.

Social media influencer marketing: Fitness influencers can demonstrate the e-commerce booking app and 24-hour access to exactly the 62% of 700 surveyed members who would pay $6 more, and engagement can be tracked. The drawbacks are slower brand building and reliance on influencer credibility, but cost per reached member is low and the app can be shown directly.

Discounted trial memberships: Free or cheap trials lower the barrier to joining and let potential members experience the 6% downtime problem for themselves; they also fill capacity quickly. However, heavy discounting reduces the $42 selling price and the $30 contribution on each membership unit, and trials may attract short-term users who never convert, worsening the 34 monthly complaints if equipment is still unreliable.

Influencers can also film the app booking journey, demonstrating the 24-hour access that 62% of members value and helping VCF justify the $42 membership price.

Recommendation: VCF should choose social media influencer marketing, supported by limited trials. It targets the surveyed segment that values 24-hour access, promotes the new app cheaply and can be scaled to two new sites. Radio is rejected as expensive and untargeted; trials alone are rejected because discounting erodes the $30 contribution and cannot fix the 34 complaints.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of the options with minimal reference to VCF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of VCF with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options with a justified recommendation explaining why radio and trials alone are rejected.

questions.question_text: VCF combines a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. Explain two benefits for VCF of this approach in dealing with 8% absenteeism and 6% equipment downtime.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Laissez-faire leadership gives gym staff freedom to rearrange shifts and cover for the 8% absenteeism themselves, which suits a workforce of 35 spread across two sites where a manager cannot be present everywhere. Greater autonomy can raise job satisfaction and commitment, reducing the 34 monthly complaints as members receive faster help with the 6% of equipment that is out of service.

Point 2: A flat structure shortens the chain of command, so a trainer who spots a faulty machine can report it and arrange a repair without waiting for several approval layers. That responsiveness is valuable with 3,600 member visits a week and an e-commerce app promising 24-hour access; it also keeps overheads low, protecting the $30 contribution on each of the 15,000 membership units. The approach also suits the laissez-faire culture: staff trusted to fix a faulty machine are more likely to take ownership of member satisfaction, which matters when 34 members complain each month and the two new gyms will need the same standards.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to VCF's absenteeism, downtime and membership data.

questions.question_text: VCF must train 9 of 35 staff on the automated access technology. Consider on-the-job training or a manufacturer course costing $420 per employee. Which should VCF choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Demonstrating the access technology on the gym floor is directly relevant to VCF's own systems, costs no fees, and keeps all 9 staff available to supervise the 3,600 weekly member visits, which matters while 6% of equipment is already out of service. It also lets trainers show staff how to handle member queries about the e-commerce app. The weakness is that trainers are operational staff whose own duties suffer, standards may vary, and there is no formal certificate.

Manufacturer course: At $420 per employee, the full 9-person course costs $3,780 (9 × $420), minor beside the $620,000 investment. It provides structured, up-to-date technical knowledge and a certificate, and takes staff away from the floor so learning is uninterrupted. However, it removes 9 of 35 staff from the two gyms temporarily, which could worsen the 8% absenteeism cover problem, and generic content may need on-site follow-up to match VCF's exact equipment.

Certification could also support the 24-hour access promise by proving that staff can operate the technology safely when no manager is on site, but VCF cannot assume the certificate reduces the 6% downtime — the insert gives no such evidence.

Decision: VCF should choose on-the-job training first, with a short manufacturer course later for the lead technicians. On-the-job training protects member service when 6% of equipment is out of service, is free and is system-specific; the full manufacturer course is rejected because removing 9 staff would deepen the 8% absence cover problem and the $3,780 fee adds cost without guaranteeing better day-to-day support.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to VCF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both methods in the context of VCF's downtime and absence.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods with a justified decision covering cost, disruption and technical relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how VCF's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $240,000 ÷ ($42 − $12) = $240,000 ÷ $30 = 8,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 8,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $42 − $12 = $30. Answer: contribution per unit is $30.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways VCF's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Comparing the 8,000-unit break-even output with 15,000 units delivered shows a margin of safety of 7,000 units, confirming the two gyms can absorb the opening costs of two more sites.
2. Contribution of $30 a unit lets managers judge the $6 premium for 24-hour access: it would raise contribution to $36 on those memberships and show how many extra members are needed to cover $240,000 fixed costs.
3. With fixed costs of $240,000 and contribution of $30, managers can set the membership volume required to service the $380,000 loan before committing further to the $620,000 expansion.
4. Average total cost ($240,000 ÷ 15,000 + $12 = $28) can be benchmarked quarterly to detect the cost of the 6% equipment downtime and to assess whether imported-equipment inflation is being controlled.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 8,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $30 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety vs 15,000-unit output; $6 premium modelling; loan-service volume for the $380,000 loan; and average total cost of $28 to monitor equipment downtime.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate VCF's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, the profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has VCF's performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 60.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 62.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 15.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 17.0%
ROCE 2024 = 12.0%
ROCE 2025 = 15.0%

Detailed workings: 2024: 720 ÷ 1,200 × 100 = 60.0%; 180 ÷ 1,200 × 100 = 15.0%; 180 ÷ 1,500 × 100 = 12.0%. 2025: 930 ÷ 1,500 × 100 = 62.0%; 255 ÷ 1,500 × 100 = 17.0%; 255 ÷ 1,700 × 100 = 15.0%. Revenue grew to $1,500,000 while cost of sales rose only to $570,000, so the first margin widened; operating profit reached $255,000. Capital employed increased to $1,700,000, yet the return on that base still improved, and interest payable fell from $36,000 to $30,000.

Evaluation: All three measures improved. The rise from 60.0% to 62.0% shows VCF is controlling direct operating costs despite 6% equipment downtime and the 11.3% imported-equipment price rise. The move from 15.0% to 17.0% indicates fixed costs of $240,000 are being spread over more of the 15,000 membership units, helped by lower interest. The return on capital employed rising from 12.0% to 15.0% is the strongest signal because it shows the larger $1,700,000 asset base is working harder, which supports the $620,000 two-site investment. A limitation is that no current assets or liabilities are given, so improved profitability does not prove VCF can meet short-term debts; the $380,000 loan still needs servicing.

Conclusion: VCF's performance has improved. Every measure rose together, and the 15.0% return on capital employed confirms that expansion is creating value rather than just adding revenue.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate percentage calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates all three measures for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost of sales, capital employed and a justified conclusion on improvement.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for VCF of charging the $6 premium for 24-hour access via the e-commerce booking app.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The survey of 700 members found that 62% would pay $6 more for 24-hour access, so the premium could lift the $42 selling price toward $48 and raise contribution per unit from $30 to $36 on those memberships. That extra contribution would help cover fixed costs of $240,000 a year, fund the $620,000 new sites and pay for repairs to the 6% of equipment out of service.

Disadvantage: the remaining members may resist paying more, and with 34 complaints a month already about service quality a higher price could raise expectations that VCF cannot meet while 6% of equipment is unavailable. The 49% who already use the app weekly may see 24-hour access as a standard feature rather than a premium one, so the surcharge could slow membership growth below the 15,000 units needed to cover costs. VCF should check whether 24-hour access can actually be delivered given the 6% equipment downtime before promoting the premium widely.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to VCF's survey, contribution and service data.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.5%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase and the 11.3% rise in imported equipment prices will affect VCF. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.0% to 4.5%): If VCF's $380,000 ten-year loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.5% of $380,000 = $1,900 a year (0.005 × $380,000). That is small next to fixed costs of $240,000, and if the loan is fixed-rate the cost is zero. Higher rates could still cool consumer spending on leisure memberships and make future finance for the $620,000 expansion dearer, but VCF can limit this by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (6.4%, to $13.62 an hour): With a workforce of 35 across two gyms, this raises wage bills for gym and reception staff and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so no annual total can be invented. The proper comparison is productivity: 15,000 units ÷ 35 staff = 428.6 units per worker, so the rise is affordable only if output per worker holds or grows; otherwise unit labour cost rises and the $30 contribution per unit is squeezed, made worse by 8% absenteeism.

Imported equipment prices (11.3%): This raises the cost of replacing the 6% of equipment out of service and of fitting out two new gyms. If the entire $620,000 investment were imported equipment, 11.3% × $620,000 = $70,060; this is an illustrative upper bound because the insert does not state the equipment share. The $12 variable cost is not decomposed, so no per-unit addition can be claimed. Growth of 4.2% in leisure spending offers some pricing room.

Conclusion: The 11.3% rise in imported equipment prices has the greatest impact. It inflates the $620,000 expansion and the replacement of faulty machines at the same time, with a possible $70,060 upper-bound effect, whereas the interest rise costs only $1,900 and the wage effect cannot be quantified from the insert and can be offset by productivity and membership growth.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to VCF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on VCF's costs, finance or revenue in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes with a well-justified judgement that equipment price inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
